```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4.5,
  fig.align = "center"
)
library(distmer)
library(vegan)
library(ggplot2)
library(kableExtra)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

Random effects describe where independent ecological replication lives. A
formula such as `(1 | site)` says that observations from the same site share a
site-level community component; it does not turn repeated quadrats or dates
into independent treatment replicates. Nested, blocked, and random-slope terms
extend that idea to more structured sampling.

`distmer` deliberately borrows `lmer` formula notation because it is a familiar and concise
way to state this hierarchy. `distmer`applies the declared fixed and random subspaces to a Gower-centred
dissimilarity matrix and obtains inference from design-appropriate
denominators and restricted permutations.

## Repeated samples within experimental units

The `vegan::pyrifos` data contain aquatic-invertebrate communities from 12
ditches sampled repeatedly before and after insecticide application. Dose was
assigned to ditches, so ditch is the experimental unit. We use four balanced
post-treatment dates per ditch.

```{r pyrifos-data}
data(pyrifos, package = "vegan")
ditch <- gl(12, 1, length = nrow(pyrifos))
week <- rep(c(-4, -1, 0.1, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 15, 19, 24), each = 12)
dose_by_ditch <- c(0.1, 0, 0, 0.9, 0, 44, 6, 0.1, 44, 0.9, 0, 6)
dose <- factor(rep(dose_by_ditch, 11))
keep <- week %in% c(1, 2, 4, 8)

community <- pyrifos[keep, ]
pyrifos_env <- data.frame(
  ditch = droplevels(ditch[keep]),
  dose = droplevels(dose[keep]),
  week = week[keep]
)
pyrifos_bray <- vegdist(community, method = "bray")
with(pyrifos_env, table(ditch, dose)) |> 
  kbl(digits=3) |> 
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed")) 
```

```{r repeated-ordination, fig.alt="Post-treatment Pyrifos samples connected through time within each ditch"}
ditch_ord <- cmdscale(pyrifos_bray, k = 2)
ditch_ord <- cbind(
  pyrifos_env,
  data.frame(Axis1 = ditch_ord[, 1], Axis2 = ditch_ord[, 2])
)

ggplot() +
  geom_path(data = ditch_ord, aes(Axis1, Axis2, group = ditch, colour = dose, order = week), alpha = 0.65, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = ditch_ord, aes(Axis1, Axis2, group = ditch, fill = dose, order = week), shape=21, alpha = 0.85) +
  coord_fixed() +
  theme_bw() + 
  scale_fill_brewer(palette="Set1") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette="Set1") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1.8, 4), breaks = c(1, 4, 8)) +
  labs(title = "Repeated community observations remain grouped by ditch",
       x = "PCoA axis 1", y = "PCoA axis 2", colour = "Dose",
       size = "Week")
```

The model is written in the same compact way as a random-intercept mixed model:

```{r random-intercept}
library(kableExtra)

ditch_fit <- permanova(
  pyrifos_bray ~ dose + (1 | ditch),
  pyrifos_env, permutations = 999, seed = 26
)

summary(ditch_fit) |> 
  kbl(digits=3) |> 
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed")) 
```

The random term also determines the denominator. Consequently, `type = "II"`
or `"III"` is not a substitute for specifying the sampling structure: when the
random design supplies an exact stratum, `type` is not applicable.

## Random slopes: each unit can change differently

A random intercept allows ditches to have different average communities. A
random slope additionally allows their within-ditch changes to differ. For a
balanced two-condition comparison, define an early and late period with two
observations in each ditch-period cell.

```{r period-data}
period_env <- transform(
  pyrifos_env,
  period = factor(
    ifelse(week %in% c(1, 2), "early", "late"),
    levels = c("early", "late")
  )
)
with(period_env, table(ditch, period)) |> 
  kbl(digits=3) |> 
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed")) 
```

```{r period-plot, fig.alt="Early to late changes on PCoA axis 1 for each Pyrifos ditch"}
period_ord <- transform(ditch_ord, period = period_env$period)
period_centres <- aggregate(
  cbind(Axis1, Axis2) ~ ditch + period,
  data = period_ord, FUN = mean
)

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = period_centres, aes(period, Axis1, group = ditch), colour = "grey65", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(data = period_centres, aes(period, Axis1, group = ditch, fill = ditch), shape=21, size = 2.4, show.legend = FALSE) +
  theme_bw() + 
  scale_fill_brewer(palette="Set1") +
  scale_color_brewer(palette="Set1") +
  labs(title = "Ditches need not share the same early-to-late change",
       x = "Period", y = "Mean PCoA axis 1 within ditch and period")
```

```{r categorical-slope}
period_fit <- permanova(
  pyrifos_bray ~ period + (1 + period | ditch),
  period_env, permutations = "all", seed = 26
)
summary(period_fit) |> 
  kbl(digits=3) |> 
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed")) 

```


A numeric gradient can also vary by unit. With four post-treatment weeks,
`(1 + week | ditch)` estimates one within-ditch community slope and tests the
equally weighted average slope against the variation among ditch slopes.

```{r continuous-slope}
continuous_fit <- permanova(
  pyrifos_bray ~ week + (1 + week | ditch),
  pyrifos_env, permutations = 999, seed = 26
)

summary(continuous_fit) |> 
  kbl(digits=3) |> 
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed")) 

```


## Translating common field designs into formulas

- `(1 | site)` — repeated observations within sites; treatments assigned among
  sites are tested with sites as the independent units.
- `(1 | region/site)` — sites nested within regions; each predictor is tested
  at the hierarchy level where it varies.
- `(1 | block) + (1 | treatment:block)` — a treatment randomized within blocks;
  the declared treatment-by-block variation supplies the treatment denominator.
- `(1 | region/site) + (1 | treatment:region) + (1 | treatment:region:site)` — treatment crossed with a nested region/site
  hierarchy.
- `(1 + condition | subject)` or `(1 + x | group)` — correlated random
  intercepts and slopes for complete repeated units.


## What `permanova()` does with the formula

For exact detail, the high-level call performs the following sequence:

1. It validates the dissimilarity and computes
   `G = -0.5 J D^2 J`. The same centring applies to every distance matrix;
   Euclidean distances give a positive semi-definite `G`, while signed axes
   from non-Euclidean distances remain in the analysis.
2. It converts fixed terms into estimable model subspaces and records whether
   each random term is a main grouping factor, a nesting declaration, an
   explicit interaction, or a random slope.
3. It checks balance, containment, crossing, cell completeness, confounding,
   and the level at which each predictor varies.
4. For supported balanced designs it derives the exact expected-mean-square
   (EMS) denominator. For supported unbalanced designs it works with equally
   weighted unit centroids or profiles and never invents an unbalanced EMS.
5. It constructs the permitted residual rearrangements, intact-unit
   permutations, or whole-unit sign flips, then reports the estimand,
   denominator, exchangeable unit, attainable permutations, and assumptions.

If no validated method matches the declared design, the model stops. A formula
that parses is not automatically a defensible permutation design.

### Implementation reference

Most users only need `permanova()`. The specialised functions below are useful
for inspecting, validating, extending a particular design, or understanding how `distmer` works:

```{r implementation-table, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
implementation <- data.frame(
  `Formula pattern` = c(
    "d ~ a",
    "d ~ a + b (unbalanced, type = )",
    "d ~ a + (1 | site)",
    "d ~ a + x + (1 | site)",
    "d ~ a + (1 | region/site)",
    "d ~ a + x + (1 | region/site)",
    "d ~ a + (1 | block) + (1 | a:block)",
    "d ~ a + (1 | region/site) + (1 | a:region) + ...",
    "d ~ x + (1 + x | group)",
    "unbalanced random / nested / block"
  ),
  `Specialised implementation` = c(
    "permanova_unbalanced(); permanova_oneway() is the direct one-factor reference",
    "permanova_unbalanced()",
    "permanova_mixed()",
    "permanova_mixed_covariate()",
    "permanova_nested()",
    "permanova_nested_covariate()",
    "permanova_crossed()",
    "permanova_hybrid()",
    "permanova_random_slope_continuous()",
    "permanova_unequal_random_intercept() / permanova_unbalanced_*()"
  ),
  `Denominator or permutation` = c(
    "Within-group residual; unrestricted observations",
    "Full-model residual; term-specific Freedman-Lane",
    "Exact whole-plot EMS",
    "Split-plot or randomized-block covariate strata",
    "Level-specific EMS; descendants move intact",
    "Covariate-adjusted nested strata",
    "Exact a:block EMS; intact cells within block",
    "Exact a:region EMS; intact treatment profiles",
    "Between-group slope; whole-group sign flips",
    "Unit-centroid inference; size- or topology-restricted permutations"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(implementation)
```
`permanova_capabilities()` returns the complete machine-readable support table,
including estimands, error-control claims, and explicit exclusions.
